claims.text: This article presents the theory, architectural decomposition, and design principles. It does not prescribe deployment mechanics; it specifies what Phase 4 adds and why it is the first explicit step toward Phase 5 goal inference and the long-range Decision Biology bridge.

claims.text: Phase 1 of the Adaptive State–Reasoning Agent (ASRA) established transition-centric experience: log every (state, action, nextstate, reward) tuple, hash grids for identity, and explore under coarse cell-diff semantics. Phase 2 added object-centric observation—connected components, transform events, and rule candidates—so that change could be described in structural vocabulary rather than pixel counts alone.

claims.text: We describe ASRA Phase 3 as the Navigation & Memory Engine: a stack that extends hash-based state graphs into exploration graphs with frontier scores, maintains visitation memory at hash and object-fingerprint resolution, separates novelty (information gain) from usefulness (progress toward reward and subgoals), tracks compositional subgoals on BabyAI and DoorKey benchmarks, reuses strategy patterns across episodes, and replays high-value transitions for analysis. The full engine lives in asra-arc/src/asra/exploration/; the Kaggle competition agent embeds a compact CompactExplorationHints module that preserves Phase 2 object-scene bias while adding visit-count novelty and loop avoidance.

claims.text: Nature Foundation Models: A Hierarchical Framework for Learning Worlds, Embodiment, and Scientific Intelligence: We propose Nature Foundation Models (NFM), a research program for systems that learn representations, dynamics, causal structure, and mechanisms directly from interaction with the natural world. NFM organizes scientific intelligence as a hierarchy—NFM-Worlds, NFM-Robotics, Atlas, and Atlas-GS—with a shared state–action–dynamics abstraction and a seven-stage developmental pipeline from world representation to adaptive scientific reasoning. The central thesis is that scientific reasoning should emerge from increasingly sophisticated interactions with learned world models rather than from an independent symbolic module.

claims.text: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language understanding, perception, planning, and control. However, most contemporary systems remain specialized architectures optimized for specific tasks, datasets, or environments. We propose Nature Foundation Models (NFM), a research program aimed at developing systems that learn representations, dynamics, causal structure, and mechanisms directly from interaction with the natural world.

claims.text: NFM introduces a hierarchical framework consisting of three layers: NFM, a general scientific intelligence research program; NFM-Worlds, a foundational world-modeling platform that learns how environments evolve through observation and intervention; and NFM-Robotics, an embodied learning platform that grounds world learning in physical interaction.

claims.text: Within this hierarchy, Atlas serves as the robotics project family, while Atlas-GS represents the first implementation based on Gaussian Splatting world representations. claims.text: Object-Centric Adaptive Reasoning: ASRA Phase 2 — From Pixel Transitions to Symbolic Structure: Phase 1 established interactive intelligence from transition evidence alone; Phase 2 adds the Observation Engine—segmentation, object alignment, transform events, and rule candidates over ARC demonstration pairs, with compact object-scene hints feeding back into the interactive agent. claims.text: Author: Ilakkuvaselvi (Ilak) Manoharan Affiliation: Nature Foundation Models Date: June 2026 Version: 1.0 — conceptual article for the Phase 2 perception track (companion to asra-phase-2-arc-prize-2026.ipynb)

claims.text: Phase 1 of the Adaptive State–Reasoning Agent (ASRA) established that interactive intelligence can begin with transition evidence alone: log state changes, infer coarse action semantics from cell-level diffs, and explore under uncertainty. That foundation is necessary but not sufficient. Human-like reasoning over grid worlds—whether static ARC puzzles or interactive ARC-style games—operates on objects, relations, and transformations, not on raw pixel arrays.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: We describe ASRA Phase 2 as the Observation Engine layer: a pipeline that segments integer grids into connected objects, detects region structure, aligns shapes across frames, classifies object-level transform events, and induces rule candidates that explain demonstration pairs. Phase 2 runs primarily on the Original ARC corpus as a supervised laboratory for abstraction; its compact object-scene representation also feeds back into the interactive agent as structural hints that bias exploration when cell counts alone are ambiguous.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: This article presents the big-picture theory, architectural decomposition, and design principles. It does not prescribe deployment mechanics; it specifies what is being built and why it sits between Phase 1 logging and later phases of memory, causality, and planning.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: ASRA’s long-range roadmap treats intelligence as a stack of competencies, each consuming the output of the previous layer:
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: text Phase 1 Experience Engine — transitions, hashes, cell diffs, exploratory policy Phase 2 Observation Engine — objects, regions, transforms, rule hypotheses Phase 3 Exploration / memory — navigation, subgoals, graph reuse Phase 4 Action semantics — causal meaning of interventions Phase 5+ Goals, planning, robustness

claims.text: Phase 1 answers: “What happened to the grid when we acted?” Phase 2 answers: “What structural entities changed, and what operator class describes that change?”

claims.text: Without Phase 2, semantics inference collapses to coarse buckets—no-op, localized update, multi-cell change—that cannot distinguish rotating a component from creating a new one, nor reuse knowledge across visually similar configurations. Phase 2 is therefore not an optional embellishment; it is the symbolization layer that makes later causal and strategic reasoning tractable.

claims.text: The agent still acts in an unknown interactive world; Phase 2 does not assume access to ground-truth object labels from the environment. On static ARC tasks, demonstration pairs (input, output) play the role of controlled experiments: each pair is one step of a latent program applied to structured input. Rule induction over demos is therefore abductive:
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: Given scenes before and after, what transformation family best explains the multiset of object events, and is that family stable across demos?
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: When demos disagree, the correct epistemic stance is not to force a single global rule at low confidence, but to emit branched per-demo hypotheses—a direct encoding of “this task is not one homogeneous operator.” That design choice mirrors human ARC solving: many puzzles combine multiple micro-rules across examples before a unifying principle becomes visible.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: Integer ARC grids use a small color palette (typically 0–15). Phase 2 adopts the standard connected-component model: pixels of equal non-background color form candidate objects. Background is estimated as the modal color unless overridden.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: In long interactive episodes, storing full pixel lists per object in every transition is wasteful. ASRA therefore distinguishes:
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: - Full scenes — used in offline ARC analysis and debugging overlays - Compact scenes — counts, bboxes, centroids, and shape hashes only; attached to transition metadata when object hints are enabled
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: Compact scenes preserve the information needed for Phase 2–style reasoning at episode scale: Did the number of objects change? Which action precedents correlate with object creation or removal?
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: Beyond objects, Phase 2 annotates regions: background, frame-like borders, and content bounding boxes. Regions anchor spatial context—useful when objects are numerous or when the grid is mostly empty. They do not replace objects; they constrain where matching and transform detection should attend.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: Given scenes ΣA and ΣB, a shape matcher aligns objects by normalized shape signatures and similarity under rotation/reflection variants. Unmatched objects in A yield DELETE events; unmatched in B yield CREATE events. Matched pairs are classified by color change, centroid displacement, and hash equality:
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: | Transform class | Typical trigger | |-----------------|-----------------| | IDENTITY | Same shape hash and color | | RECOLOR | Same shape, different color | | TRANSLATE | Matched shape, centroid shift | | ROTATE / REFLECT | Shape equivalence up to symmetry group | | CREATE / DELETE | Unmatched object | | COMPOSE | Multiple event types in one pair |
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: A pair’s summary aggregates the event multiset (e.g., “12 events: CREATE, DELETE, ROTATE”). This is the bridge from geometry to language-ready tokens for rule induction.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: The Phase 2 baseline is heuristic, not complete. Recolor and reflection may collapse into rotate/identity when shape hashes align. Large grids with many small components produce noisy event counts. The evaluation corpus (800 Original ARC tasks) shows DELETE/CREATE/ROTATE dominating aggregate statistics—consistent with greedy matching and recomposition-heavy puzzles, not with human-level program synthesis.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: Phase 2 metrics measure perception coverage and demo consistency, not test-set solve rate. That distinction is intentional: the Observation Engine must be measurable before it is asked to drive a winning game agent.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: 5. Rule induction and branched hypotheses
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: From a list of per-demo transform detections, the generator proposes templates:
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: 1. Global common rule — if every demo shares the same transform-type set, emit APPLY{TYPES}TOMATCHEDOBJECTS with confidence 1.0. 2. Per-object marginal rules — PEROBJECTROTATE, etc., with support = fraction of demos exhibiting that type. 3. Branched model — when demo summaries diverge, emit BRANCHEDPERDEMO plus PERDEMO{i}{DOMINANTTYPES} for each demonstration index.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: The branched form resolves a systematic failure mode: ~2% of ARC training tasks (and a similar fraction of evaluation tasks) previously showed top rules with confidence below 1.0 not because parsing failed, but because cross-demo operator heterogeneity was real. Encoding branches explicitly turns inconsistency into structure instead of noise.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: High confidence indicates internal consistency of the heuristic rule template across demos, not correctness on hidden test outputs. It is a consistency score for the perception stack’s own abstractions—a prerequisite for downstream solvers, not a substitute for them.
topics: object-centric adaptive reasoning: asra phase 2 — from pixel transitions to symbolic structure

claims.text: We present Orbit Wars Phase 4, an open-source Kaggle competition agent that unifies three research frameworks—Nature Foundation Models (NFM), Adaptive Scientific Reasoning Architecture (ASRA), and Atlas-GS—within a real-time strategy environment. Orbit Wars is a continuous 2D multi-agent game where bots send fleets across an orbiting solar system to capture planets, intercept comets, and maximize ship count over 500 turns under a one-second-per-turn decision budget. Phase 4 maps NFM's state–action–dynamics abstraction to explicit world-state transitions, adapts Atlas-GS Gaussian spatial splatting as a 2D production-value field for target prioritization, and implements ASRA's Observe → Hypothesize → Experiment → Analyze → Act loop via five strategic hypotheses tested through 15-turn forward simulation. The agent builds on Phase 2's simulation core (best ladder score μ=600 in prior submissions) while replacing naive nearest-neighbor targeting with spatially-aware economic reasoning and hypothesis-driven policy selection. Code is open-sourced at github.com/ilakkmanoharan/orbit-wars.

claims.text: Adaptive intelligence in unfamiliar environments cannot begin with predefined policies. The environment does not publish action manuals, win conditions, or transition rules. ASRA Phase 1 establishes the Experience Engine — a minimal agent architecture that treats every intervention as an experiment: observe grid state, apply an action token, measure cell-level diffs and reward proxies, accumulate transition evidence, infer coarse action semantics conditioned on state identity, and explore under uncertainty while tabooing empirically dead ends.

claims.text: We describe Phase 1 as the foundation layer of the Adaptive Scientific Reasoning Architecture: transition logging (τ = (s, a, s′, r)), hash-stable state IDs, effect-based semantics inference, information-directed exploration, Swarm-scale multi-game orchestration, and competition-grade execution fidelity (isolated venv, validation vs. scoring separation). The research library lives in asra-arc/ (env/, memory/, agent/); the Kaggle agent embeds a compact ASRAAgent with ActionSemanticsInferencer and ASRAExplorer.

Nature Foundation Models (NFM) is a research program for learning persistent world models, action semantics, causal structure, and mechanisms from interaction—a hierarchy from NFM through NFM-Worlds, NFM-Robotics, Atlas, and Atlas-GS v1, connected to the nine-phase ASRA adaptive scientific reasoning stack and Decision Biology.

Understanding Action Semantics Inference Through State Transitions in ASRA: Explains how ASRA discovers what actions mean without being told—using a simple 3×3 grid example (Before → ACTION → After), change detection, semantic convergence, and a concrete update rule—then connects it to ARC reasoning, world models, Decision Biology, and the ASRA loop.

Nature Foundation Models, Decision Biology, and A-S-R-A — Adaptive Scientific Intelligence: Technical overview (~10 min) of the research stack: why current AI is insufficient for scientific discovery, what Nature Foundation Models aim to build, how Decision Biology reframes cells as information-processing agents, and how A‑S‑R‑A learns hidden action semantics and evolving world models through interaction.

ASRA Phase 1: First 10 Replay Frames — Guided Tutorial: Walkthrough of ASRA Phase 1 replay frames: before/after grids, changed cells, movement labels, and the on‑screen formula preview—clarifying that the mock backend cycles color in fixed cells (not spatial movement).

ASRA Phase 1: Animated Replay Walkthrough — How the Agent Sees, Acts, and Remembers: Narrated tour of the Phase 1 Animated Replay viewer: how episodes auto-play, how diffs are highlighted, why early RESET steps may show no change, and how replay ties to memory-on-disk and later learning.

I'm building Nature Foundation Models — a company focused on a problem most AI systems still get wrong: scientific reasoning under uncertainty.

Today, the best models in biology and science are extraordinarily good at pattern prediction. They are much weaker at what actual science requires: choosing interventions, learning causal structure, updating beliefs from experiments, and discovering hidden mechanisms in unfamiliar systems.

That gap is expensive. Drug discovery, target validation, and biological research still depend on slow, manual experimentation because our AI stack was built for static datasets—not for closed-loop scientific inquiry.
At the center is ASRA (Adaptive Scientific Reasoning Architecture): a reasoning engine for world-model construction, causal inference, intervention learning, and adaptive experimentation.
Our first domain is Decision Biology — treating cells as adaptive decision systems that process signals, respond to perturbations, and evolve under uncertainty. We model:
- perturbations as interventions - signaling pathways as world models - cellular adaptation as causal reasoning

This is not another LLM wrapper or prediction pipeline. ASRA is designed to learn what actions mean from interaction itself—then use that understanding to propose, test, and revise scientific hypotheses.
Long term, Nature Foundation Models becomes a multi-domain scientific intelligence platform spanning biology, chemistry, physics, and environmental systems.

1. Foundation models proved that large-scale representation learning works at scale. 2. Biology is becoming an intervention-rich state space — single-cell atlases, perturbation compendia (LINCS, scPerturb), and multimodal datasets make closed-loop reasoning possible for the first time. 3. Scientific AI is shifting from prediction toward reasoning, agents, and experimentation — but most systems still assume predefined action spaces and known environment semantics.
We believe the next major platform opportunity is not a bigger chat model. It is infrastructure for machines that reason about nature the way scientists do.

I've spent nearly 20 years building production systems across AI, distributed infrastructure, cloud, and scientific computing. Over the past year I've been working full-time on ASRA, Decision Biology, and the research foundation behind Nature Foundation Models:

- Published conceptual architecture and research direction (including a review on adaptive scientific reasoning under uncertainty) - Early prototypes: transition logging, world-model experiments, adaptive reasoning loops - Public research repo and domain site live today

I'm not optimizing for a demo that looks smart on a slide. I'm building the cognitive substrate for scientific intelligence — the kind of foundational work that compounds into breakthrough products over a decade, not a quarter.

The core business is foundational STEM research — world models, causal inference, intervention semantics, uncertainty-aware experimentation, and scientific representation learning across natural systems.
That research produces the compounding asset. Downstream, it enables side products and platform revenue:
- scientific reasoning infrastructure - adaptive research platforms - domain-specific scientific foundation models - enterprise scientific AI and autonomous experimentation systems
Decision Biology is the wedge. Nature Foundation Models is the platform.

If you're looking for the next infrastructure-layer bet in AI — not application-layer copilots, but the system that makes scientific discovery itself more adaptive — I'd welcome 20 minutes to walk you through the architecture, research, and roadmap.

Hi Jason — congrats on wrapping LA36. Year zero / year one support is the hardest work in this business, and I appreciate that Launch makes space for founders still early in that journey.

I applied to YC S26 for Nature Foundation Models (currently under Bubbles & Cafe Inc. — renaming soon) and haven't heard back yet. YC has been a long-standing dream for me — not as a credential, but as the environment this company needs: ambitious peers, relentless focus on what matters, and a community that gets deep, long-horizon technical work. I'm building either way, but I'd also sincerely welcome the chance to talk with you about Launch.

Nature Foundation Models — adaptive scientific intelligence for natural systems. Most AI in science optimizes pattern prediction. Real discovery needs choosing interventions, learning causal structure, updating beliefs from experiments, and finding hidden mechanisms under uncertainty.
At the center is ASRA (Adaptive Scientific Reasoning Architecture): world-model construction, causal inference, intervention learning, adaptive experimentation.

First domain: Decision Biology — cells as adaptive decision systems. Perturbations as interventions, signaling pathways as world models, cellular adaptation as causal reasoning. Not another LLM wrapper — ASRA learns what actions mean from interaction, then proposes, tests, and revises hypotheses.
Long term: multi-domain scientific intelligence across biology, chemistry, physics, and environmental systems. Decision Biology is the wedge; Nature Foundation Models is the platform.

Why now: foundation models proved representation learning at scale; biology is becoming intervention-rich (single-cell atlases, perturbation compendia); scientific AI is shifting from prediction toward reasoning — but most systems still assume predefined action spaces.

Where I am: ~20 years in production AI, distributed infra, cloud, and scientific computing. Recently full-time on ASRA and the research foundation — published architecture and direction, early prototypes (transition logging, world-model experiments, adaptive reasoning loops), public repo and site live. Solo founder, year zero.
Happy to forward my YC application, share a deck, or jump on a call.

I am writing to express my strong interest in joining OpenAI Robotics. I have been deeply inspired by OpenAI’s vision of building AI systems that can meaningfully interact with and assist people in the physical world, and I would be excited to contribute across robotics, world models, scientific reasoning, and adaptive intelligence systems.

I am a software engineer and independent researcher with experience spanning distributed systems, AI systems, mobile and backend engineering, cloud infrastructure, and scientific AI architectures. Over the past several years, I have been increasingly focused on foundational research directions involving adaptive reasoning systems, world models, hidden mechanism inference, and scientific intelligence.

https://ilakk-manoharan.vercel.app/exceptional-ability

Adaptive scientific reasoning (ARC Prize 2026 & Decision Biology) Recently, I started working on the Kaggle Competition ARC Prize 2026 — ARC-AGI-3, and immediately wanted to apply world models to Decision Biology and Nature Foundation Models too.

The idea of agents exploring unfamiliar environments, inferring hidden mechanics, learning action semantics, and building adaptive reasoning systems felt directly connected to biological systems and cellular decision-making.

So far, a lot of computational biology has mainly focused on prediction, classification, statistical modeling, sequence analysis, and narrow ML applications on biological datasets. But biological systems are adaptive, dynamic, uncertain, and continuously interacting with their environments.

What became very exciting to me is the possibility of using world models, adaptive reasoning, hidden-state inference, and exploration-driven learning to model how cells process information, respond to perturbations, adapt, and make decisions under uncertainty.

Currently I'm building ASRA — an adaptive reasoning engine; Decision Biology — the first scientific domain built on top of it; and Nature Foundation Models — a broader scientific intelligence platform across biology, chemistry, physics, and environmental systems.

ASRA on GitHub: https://github.com/ilakkmanoharan/asra ARC Prize 2026 — ARC-AGI-3: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3 I am currently developing a research framework called ASRA (Adaptive Scientific Reasoning Architectures), which explores how adaptive systems can gradually infer structure, semantics, and causal dynamics of unfamiliar environments through interaction itself. The work is closely related to topics such as:

world models and latent environment representations, action semantics inference, transition and state differencing, intervention learning, causal abstraction, replay and reflection systems, adaptive exploration under uncertainty, and autonomous mechanism discovery. On top of ASRA, I am also exploring:

Decision Biology — adaptive reasoning and information-processing systems for biological environments, and Nature Foundation Models — broader scientific intelligence systems spanning biology, physics, environmental systems, and adaptive experimentation. I am particularly interested in how robotics systems can evolve beyond predefined semantic assumptions and develop richer internal models of physical environments through continual interaction and experimentation.
Recently, I have also been exploring areas related to:

Gaussian Splatting, embodied world models, 3D scene understanding, environment reconstruction, spatial reasoning, and adaptive multimodal systems for robotics and scientific discovery. My background includes approximately 20 years of engineering experience across software systems, cloud infrastructure, APIs, mobile applications, AI systems, and distributed architectures. I enjoy working across the stack and building systems end-to-end.

ASRA — Adaptive Scientific Reasoning Architecture

ASRA is a modular cognitive architecture for fluid intelligence in unfamiliar interactive environments. It studies adaptive reasoning, hypothesis-driven exploration, world-model formation, and reusable abstraction memory. Inspired by ARC-AGI-3, it treats intelligence as rapid adaptation—not memorization, fixed policies, or static prediction. The system behaves like a scientist: observe, form hypotheses, experiment, analyze outcomes, and refine internal theories. A recursive loop—observe → hypothesize → experiment → analyze → refine → retry—governs interaction with novel environments. ASRA targets unseen tasks, hidden mechanics, sparse information, and uncertain action semantics under exploration-driven learning. Modular subsystems (observation, hypothesis, experimentation, analysis, world models, abstraction memory, reflection) cooperate through one orchestrated cycle. It aligns with ARC-AGI-3: exploration, memory, sequential reasoning, and generalization in interactive settings—not static puzzle solving. Memory stores reasoning concepts and abstractions, not task-specific answers; exploration is hypothesis-driven, not brute force. Research asks whether agents can invent strategies dynamically, build compact theories of new worlds, and transfer abstractions across tasks. Core stance: adaptation over memorization, scientific reasoning over search, world understanding over output prediction, generalization over benchmark fitting. Positioning: A fluid-intelligence architecture for adaptive scientific reasoning, exploration, and strategy invention in unseen environments. Tagline: A fluid-intelligence architecture for adaptive scientific reasoning in unseen interactive environments.

Many current papers optimize agent infrastructure.

claims.text: We present ARC-Genome, a neural circuit compiler for the NeuroGolf 2026 Kaggle competition (IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Competitions Track). The competition asks a question distinct from ARC Prize: not merely can you solve the task? but what is the cheapest neural network that implements the transformation? Our approach treats each ARC-AGI task as a program to be inferred and compiled into a minimal ONNX graph, rather than a dataset to be trained on.
topics: arc-genome: minimal neural circuits for arc-agi

claims.text: Over six incremental phases and two milestones, we built a cost-aware synthesis pipeline with 11+ analytical solvers, convolutional fallbacks, composition search, and ARC-GEN synthetic validation. Our central discovery is that raw solve count is a misleading metric: of 199 locally "solved" tasks in Phase 6, only 23 generalized to ARC-GEN variants and earned Kaggle points—exactly matching our leaderboard score of 388.20. Re-solving with ARC-GEN gating raised verified tasks to 52 with an estimated score of 843. This paper documents the competition, our methodology, each development phase, and what we have accomplished.

claims.text: ARC-Genome reframes NeuroGolf as a compilation problem: infer the transformation, emit the minimal circuit, verify generalization. Our six-phase development taught us that the competition punishes conv overfitting severely—only 12% of locally solved tasks actually earn points. Milestone 1b demonstrates that enforcing ARC-GEN validation during synthesis, not just audit, can more than double verified score while submitting fewer files.

claims.text: ASRA-Security is an algorithmic red-teaming system submitted to the Kaggle competition AI Agent Security - Multi-Step Tool Attacks, hosted by OpenAI, Google, and IEEE. The project reframes agent security as sequential decision-making under a search budget: an attack algorithm interacts with a deterministic sandbox environment, explores multi-step tool-use trajectories, and returns replayable attack candidates that an independent evaluator can verify.
topics: asra-security: adaptive search for multi-step tool-using agent failures

claims.text: Rather than crafting single-shot jailbreak prompts, ASRA-Security combines Go-Explore-style archive search, a novelty archive over tool-call cell signatures, heuristic trace scoring aligned with competition security predicates, and prompt mutation over curated benchmark seeds. The implementation is packaged as a Kaggle code submission (attack.py + inference-server notebook) and is open-sourced on GitHub.

claims.text: Modern AI agents increasingly operate through tools: reading email, searching the web, writing files, posting HTTP data, and executing commands. These capabilities create multi-step failure modes that single-prompt safety tests cannot fully capture. A harmful instruction embedded in an email or webpage may be ingested in one step and only trigger an unsafe action several tool calls later.

claims.text: 1. Seed the archive with an initial interaction from curated benchmark prompts. 2. Select an archive entry using weighted sampling over visit count, score hint, and depth. 3. Score each resulting trace; add novel cells to the archive. 6. Collect replayable candidates when predicates fire on novel signatures. 7. Repeat until the time budget or step limit is exhausted. 8. Return deduplicated, ranked, capped findings via finalizefindings().

ARC-Genome (ARC-NeuroGolf) — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: We present ARC-Genome, a neural circuit compiler for the NeuroGolf 2026 Kaggle competition (IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Competitions Track). The competition asks a question distinct from ARC Prize: not merely can you solve the task? but what is the cheapest neural network that implements the transformation? Our approach treats each ARC-AGI task as a program to be inferred and compiled into a minimal ONNX graph, rather than a dataset to be trained on.

ARC-Genome (ARC-NeuroGolf) — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: Over six incremental phases and two milestones, we built a cost-aware synthesis pipeline with 11+ analytical solvers, convolutional fallbacks, composition search, and ARC-GEN synthetic validation. Our central discovery is that raw solve count is a misleading metric: of 199 locally "solved" tasks in Phase 6, only 23 generalized to ARC-GEN variants and earned Kaggle points—exactly matching our leaderboard score of 388.20. Re-solving with ARC-GEN gating raised verified tasks to 52 with an estimated score of 843. This paper documents the competition, our methodology, each development phase, and what we have accomplished.

ARC-Genome (ARC-NeuroGolf) — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: The 2026 NeuroGolf Championship is a Kaggle research competition with $50,000 in prizes, affiliated with IJCAI-ECAI 2026. Participants must solve tasks from the ARC-AGI public training set v1—400 grid-transformation puzzles—and submit one ONNX neural network per task.

ARC-Genome (ARC-NeuroGolf) — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: ARC-Genome reframes NeuroGolf as a compilation problem: infer the transformation, emit the minimal circuit, verify generalization. Our six-phase development taught us that the competition punishes conv overfitting severely—only 12% of locally solved tasks actually earn points. Milestone 1b demonstrates that enforcing ARC-GEN validation during synthesis, not just audit, can more than double verified score while submitting fewer files.

The remaining gap to leaderboard class (~7,700) is analytical coverage: discovering and compiling the structural rules that hundreds of ARC tasks share, rather than fitting them away with convolution.

Nature Foundation Models — Atlas-GS — Atlas-GS Implementation Guide: For each observation, valid depth pixels are back-projected with intrinsics and transformed to world frame using GT or estimated pose. Stride=2 subsampling for speed.

Nature Foundation Models — Atlas-GS — Atlas-GS Implementation Guide: Points are aggregated into voxels of size mapping.voxelsize (default 2 cm). Each voxel becomes one Gaussian with mean position, mean color, mean opacity, isotropic scale ≈ voxel/2.
Nature Foundation Models — Atlas-GS — Atlas-GS Implementation Guide: New keyframe when translation ≥ 8 cm or rotation ≥ 8° vs last keyframe (configurable).

Nature Foundation Models — Atlas-GS — Atlas-GS Implementation Guide: Initialize from GT pose (TUM) or previous frame. Subsampled depth points refined with lightweight ICP against Gaussian centers (max correspondence 5 cm, 30 iterations).
Nature Foundation Models — Atlas-GS — Atlas-GS Implementation Guide: Consecutive GT poses → basevelocity action with Δtranslation; JSONL append-only log for v2 action semantics.

Ilakk Manoharan Portfolio — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: We present ARC-Genome, a neural circuit compiler for the NeuroGolf 2026 Kaggle competition (IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Competitions Track). The competition asks a question distinct from ARC Prize: not merely can you solve the task? but what is the cheapest neural network that implements the transformation? Our approach treats each ARC-AGI task as a program to be inferred and compiled into a minimal ONNX graph, rather than a dataset to be trained on.

Ilakk Manoharan Portfolio — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: Over six incremental phases and two milestones, we built a cost-aware synthesis pipeline with 11+ analytical solvers, convolutional fallbacks, composition search, and ARC-GEN synthetic validation. Our central discovery is that raw solve count is a misleading metric: of 199 locally "solved" tasks in Phase 6, only 23 generalized to ARC-GEN variants and earned Kaggle points—exactly matching our leaderboard score of 388.20. Re-solving with ARC-GEN gating raised verified tasks to 52 with an estimated score of 843. This paper documents the competition, our methodology, each development phase, and what we have accomplished.

Ilakk Manoharan Portfolio — ARC-Genome: Minimal Neural Circuits for ARC-AGI: The 2026 NeuroGolf Championship is a Kaggle research competition with $50,000 in prizes, affiliated with IJCAI-ECAI 2026. Participants must solve tasks from the ARC-AGI public training set v1—400 grid-transformation puzzles—and submit one ONNX neural network per task.

Cost — Score is logarithmic in circuit size; a hand-compiled color map (~100 bytes) beats a 29×29 convolution (~10⁷ MACs) by orders of magnitude.

Orbit Wars (local repo orbit-wars): Phased, open-source AI agent pipeline for Kaggle's Orbit Wars RTS competition ($50K prize pool): continuous 2D space, orbiting planets, comets, and multi-agent FFA under a one-second turn budget. Five versioned phases—from baseline ladder bot (μ 505.8) through intercept geometry, six-policy forward simulation, competition meta, and Phase 4 unifying NFM × ASRA × Atlas-GS.

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: Phase 0 establishes the development environment, validates the submission pipeline, and deploys a minimal working bot to the Kaggle ladder. The goal is not strength — it is to confirm that your agent runs under competition constraints and begins accumulating skill-rating episodes immediately.

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: | Artifact | Purpose | |---|---| | main.py | Competition-ready agent (baseline expander) | | runlocal.py | Local smoke test against random | | This paper | Documents setup steps and design rationale |

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: 1. Join the competition at kaggle.com/competitions/orbit-wars and accept the rules before the entry deadline (June 16, 2026). 2. Install dependencies: bash pip install "kaggle-environments=1.28.0" kaggle 3. Configure Kaggle CLI — save your API token to ~/.kaggle/accesstoken or run kaggle auth login. 4. Run local smoke test: bash python phase0/runlocal.py 5. Submit to the ladder: bash kaggle competitions submit orbit-wars -f phase0/main.py -m "phase0 baseline v1"
Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: The Phase 0 bot implements the competition starter pattern with three safety guards:
Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: For each owned planet with surplus ships, find the nearest planet not owned by the player and launch enough ships to capture it (target.ships + 1).
Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: Never drain a planet below 5 ships. This prevents home-planet snipes and avoids sending fleets so small they move at minimum speed (1 unit/turn).

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: Before launching, check whether the straight-line path from the planet edge to the target crosses the sun (center at (50, 50), radius 10). Fleets crossing the sun are destroyed — skipping these launches prevents silent ship loss.

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: The evaluation system gives newly submitted bots more frequent episodes for faster rating feedback. A weak but valid bot on the ladder is more valuable than a perfect bot submitted on the last day with no rating history.

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: Phase 0 does not predict orbiting planet positions, prioritize production value, or plan ahead. It will lose to any bot that does. Phases 1–3 address these gaps progressively.

Orbit Wars — Phase 0: Setup & First Submission: - [ ] Local test completes without errors - [ ] Kaggle validation episode passes (self-play) - [ ] Submission appears on the Submissions page with status other than Error - [ ] Average turn time well under 1 second

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: Phase 1 replaces naive nearest-neighbor expansion with a production-aware, geometry-informed heuristic. The bot should consistently beat random agents and weak baselines without any forward simulation or machine learning.

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: | Feature | Phase 0 | Phase 1 | |---|---|---| | Target selection | Nearest planet | Highest production / (eta + 1) score | | Garrison policy | Fixed 5 ships | max(3, production) per planet | | Moving targets | Aims at current position | Predicts orbit position at fleet arrival | | Sun avoidance | Yes | Yes (shared geometry module) | | Comets | Ignored | Basic intercept when comets are active |

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: phase1/ paper.md ← this document geometry.py ← orbit prediction, fleet speed, ETA, sun check agent.py ← heuristic decision loop main.py ← Kaggle entry point runlocal.py ← local test runner
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: Fleet speed follows the competition formula:
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: speed = 1.0 + (maxSpeed - 1.0) (log(ships) / log(1000))^1.5
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: Larger fleets arrive faster but leave the source planet more exposed. Phase 1 sends the minimum ships needed to capture rather than half the garrison.

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: Inner planets (where orbitalradius + planetradius < 50) rotate around the sun at angularvelocity radians per turn. Given a planet's entry in initialplanets, we compute:
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: currentangle = initialangle + angularvelocity stepdelta position = (CENTER + rcos(angle), CENTER + rsin(angle))
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: To intercept a moving planet, we iterate turn-by-turn:

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: 1. Advance fleet position by fleetspeed(ships) along the launch angle. 2. Advance target planet position by one rotation step. 3. Stop when distance ≤ planet radius (collision).
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: The launch angle is recomputed each iteration toward the predicted target position (pursuit guidance).
Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: Before committing a launch, we verify the path from spawn point to target does not pass within SUNRADIUS of (50, 50).

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: 1. Parses planets, fleets, comets, and player ID from the observation. 2. Computes a minimum garrison for each owned planet: max(3, production). 3. Scores every attackable target: - Neutrals: production / (eta + 1) — high production close by wins. - Enemy planets: same formula, but only if we have ≥ 1.5× required ships (avoid costly trades). 4. Greedy assignment: best (source, target) pairs are executed until planets run out of surplus ships. 5. Comet bonus: if active comets exist, boost score for nearby comets we can reach within 30 turns.

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: - Production is king: A production-5 planet generates 5 ships/turn. Capturing it early compounds over 500 turns. - Minimum capture force: Sending garrison + 1 ships minimizes exposure while guaranteeing capture against neutrals. - No over-commitment on enemies: Attacking only with overwhelming force avoids pyrrhic victories in multi-fleet combat.

Orbit Wars — Phase 1: Strong Heuristic Bot: - Greedy assignment can send multiple fleets to the same target in one turn (wasted in multi-attacker combat). - No lookahead — a patient opponent can out-expand on the far side of the map. - Phase 2 addresses this with simulation.

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: Phase 2 adds forward simulation to choose among candidate move sets each turn. Instead of committing to a single greedy heuristic, the bot evaluates several strategies by rolling the game state forward 10–15 turns and picking the opening moves that maximize a hand-crafted value function.
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: Heuristic bots are reactive — they make locally optimal decisions without considering how the board evolves. Common failure modes:

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: - Sending a fleet that arrives after an enemy reinforcement - Over-expanding toward one quadrant while neutrals in another go uncontested - Draining home planet garrison before a counter-attack lands
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: Lightweight simulation catches these by projecting consequences before acting.

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: phase2/ paper.md geometry.py ← shared with Phase 1 (orbit, ETA, sun) simulation.py ← simplified forward model + value function agent.py ← policy picker: generate candidates → simulate → pick best main.py runlocal.py

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: The simulator is intentionally simplified — it does not replicate every game rule exactly, but captures enough dynamics for relative comparison between candidate policies.
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: A SimState holds: - Planet list (id, owner, x, y, radius, ships, production) - Active fleets (owner, x, y, angle, ships) - Current step counter

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: 1. Production — owned planets generate ships. 2. Apply our moves — launch fleets from specified move list. 3. Opponent model — each enemy/neutral planet with surplus sends half its garrison toward the nearest neutral (crude but sufficient for comparison). 4. Fleet movement — move all fleets one step; resolve planet collisions with simplified combat (attackerships - garrison, capture if positive). 5. Planet rotation — update orbiting planet positions.
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: score = sum(production for owned planets) 10 + sum(ships on owned planets) + sum(ships in owned fleets) + 5 count(owned planets)
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: Production is weighted heavily because it represents future ship income over the remaining game.
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: Each turn, generate candidate move sets from distinct strategies:

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: | Policy | Behavior | |---|---| | expandneutrals | Phase 1 heuristic restricted to neutral targets only | | expandall | Phase 1 heuristic on all targets | | snipeweakest | Attack the enemy planet with lowest garrison | | reinforcehome | Send surplus from outer planets toward highest-production owned planet | | cometrush | Prioritize capturable comets | | conservative | Only expand to neutrals within ETA ≤ 20, keep 2× garrison floor |

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: For each candidate: 1. Clone current state. 2. Apply candidate moves for turn 0. 3. Simulate 12 turns with the opponent model handling enemy/neutral reactions. 4. Record the value function score.
Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: Execute the first turn's moves from the highest-scoring candidate.

Orbit Wars — Phase 2: Simulation & Search: With 6 candidates × 12 turns × ~40 planets, simulation stays under ~100 ms on typical hardware — well within the 1-second turn limit. If needed, reduce SIMDEPTH or candidate count.

Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: The agent classifies each turn into one of three phases:

Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: Opening (steps 0–80) - Prioritize high-production neutrals. - Keep home garrison at max(5, production 2). - Ignore enemy planets unless extremely weak (≤ 5 ships).

Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: Midgame (steps 81–350) - Full policy picker from Phase 2. - Comet windows: during 10 steps before each comet spawn, boost cometrush weight. - FFA check: if ≥ 2 enemies have more total ships than us, prefer expandneutrals over snipeweakest.

Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: Endgame (steps 351–500) - If our ship count ≥ 1.2× the second-place estimate, use conservative only. - Otherwise continue midgame policies but avoid reinforcing enemies by attacking fortified planets.
Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: Each turn, estimate total ships per player:
Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: total = sum(planet.ships for owned planets) + sum(fleet.ships for owned fleets)
Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: In FFA, attacking the weakest enemy is only preferred when we are not the weakest player overall.
Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: Comets spawn at steps [50, 150, 250, 350, 450]. During steps spawn - 10 through spawn - 1:
Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: 1. Parse obs["comets"] for incoming path endpoints. 2. Boost comet target scores by 3×. 3. Launch from the nearest owned planet with surplus ≥ 10 ships.
Orbit Wars — Phase 3: Polish & Meta-Strategy: Comets have production 1 but are free captures — valuable for ship count tiebreakers.
